content: Cough is a frequent symptom in children, often leading to increased healthcare visits and significant burden on parents. Chronic cough, defined as a cough lasting four weeks or longer, may indicate serious underlying conditions such as an inhaled foreign body or bronchiectasis. Codeine and its derivatives are sometimes used to treat cough due to their antitussive (cough-suppressing) properties. However, these medications carry significant risks, including suppression of respiratory drive, anaphylaxis triggered by anesthesia, and potential for addiction. Children are particularly vulnerable to these side effects due to variability in metabolic response and dosage sensitivity. A systematic review of the available evidence is necessary to guide clinical management of chronic cough in children. The objective of this review was to assess the safety and efficacy of codeine and its derivatives in treating chronic cough in children. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Airways Group Register of Trials, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE, and online trial registries such as those maintained by the World Health Organization and ClinicalTrials.gov. No language restrictions were applied. Studies were considered eligible if they included children under 18 years of age with chronic cough lasting four weeks or more and if they compared codeine or its derivatives to placebo in a randomized controlled trial design. Two independent reviewers screened the search results against standardized criteria. A total of 556 records were identified, of which 486 were excluded based on title and abstract. The remaining 70 references were reviewed in full, but none met the inclusion criteria. Consequently, no evidence was found to either support or oppose the use of codeine or its derivatives as antitussive agents for chronic cough in children. Although chronic cough differs from acute cough, systematic reviews on the use of codeine for acute cough in children have similarly found no evidence to support or oppose the use of over-the-counter cough and cold medications containing codeine or its derivatives. This lack of evidence has been consistently reaffirmed by international chronic cough guidelines and by regulatory authorities in the USA, Europe, Canada, New Zealand, and Australia. Due to the absence of evidence supporting efficacy and the known risks associated with codeine use—particularly in children—these medications are no longer recommended for children under 12 years of age or for those aged 12 to 18 years with respiratory conditions. In conclusion, this review underscores the lack of randomized controlled trials evaluating the use of codeine-based medications for chronic cough in children. Given the potential for serious adverse effects, including respiratory suppression and opioid toxicity, national regulatory authorities advise against the use of codeine in children under 12 years of age. Clinical practice should align with established guidelines, avoiding the use of codeine or its derivatives for treating cough in children. Instead, management should focus on addressing the underlying cause of chronic cough.
